question: What happens when conflicts between healthcare workers are left unresolved?

options.A: Improved compliance with annual hospital policies
options.B: Increased funding for hospital equipment and supplies
options.C: Compromised patient safety and lower staff morale
options.D: Faster turnaround times for patient discharges

explanation: When team members stay at odds, communication breaks down. This distracts everyone and puts patient care at risk while making work feel miserable. [learn more](GST321_U5_T4#GST321_U5_T4_h1)

question: In what way can a healthy disagreement actually help a nursing unit?

options.A: By completely eliminating the need for multidisciplinary meetings
options.B: By ensuring all nurses agree on every clinical decision
options.C: By reducing the total number of daily patient admissions
options.D: By encouraging creative problem-solving and exposing workflow flaws

explanation: Not all conflict is bad! Healthy debates let team members point out broken workflows and find smarter, safer ways to care for patients. [learn more](GST321_U5_T4#GST321_U5_T4_h1)

question: Which of these is a common reason why conflicts start in a hospital ward?

options.A: Ambiguous roles and unclear scopes of practice
options.B: Too many open nursing positions on the ward
options.C: An excess of available medical equipment
options.D: Identical personalities among all staff members

explanation: When people aren't quite sure where their duties end and someone else's begin, misunderstandings and friction are bound to happen. [learn more](GST321_U5_T4#GST321_U5_T4_h2)

question: A nurse and a doctor argue because both want to decide the exact time to discharge a patient. What is the root cause here?

options.A: An absolute surplus of transport vehicles
options.D: A complete lack of patient admission records

explanation: When two professionals clash over who has the final say, it usually means their job boundaries overlap and power is being contested. [learn more](GST321_U5_T4#GST321_U5_T4_h2)

question: The Thomas-Kilmann conflict model is built on which two main personal behaviors?
explanation: This model simply looks at two things: how much you push for your own needs versus how much you try to help the other person. [learn more](GST321_U5_T4#GST321_U5_T4_h3)

question: How does the 'collaborating' style work in the Thomas-Kilmann model?

options.A: It gives up complete control just to keep the peace on the ward.
options.B: It prioritizes personal victory over the needs of everyone else involved.
options.C: It uses low assertiveness and low cooperativeness to ignore the problem entirely.
options.D: It combines high assertiveness with high cooperativeness to find a win-win solution.

explanation: Collaboration is all about working together closely so both sides feel fully heard and completely satisfied with the result. [learn more](GST321_U5_T4#GST321_U5_T4_h3)

question: What is the biggest plus of using a collaborating conflict style?

options.A: It produces a win-win solution that addresses the root cause
options.B: It forces one party to surrender completely
options.D: It requires very little time during a busy shift

explanation: It takes time and patience, but collaboration gets to the bottom of the issue so everyone wins. [learn more](GST321_U5_T4#GST321_U5_T4_h4)

question: When is compromising a better choice than collaborating?

options.A: When unlimited time is available for deep discussion
options.B: When time is limited and a quick middle ground is needed
options.C: When patient safety is directly and immediately threatened
options.D: When neither party cares about the final outcome

explanation: When you are rushed on the ward and don't have hours to talk things through, splitting the difference (compromising) is a fast, practical fix. [learn more](GST321_U5_T4#GST321_U5_T4_h4)

question: When is a 'competing' (directive) conflict style actually the right move in a hospital?

options.A: When discussing break schedules with colleagues
options.B: During emergency resuscitation or immediate safety threats

explanation: In an emergency like a code blue, there's no time to debate. A strong leader needs to take charge immediately to keep the patient safe. [learn more](GST321_U5_T4#GST321_U5_T4_h5)

question: What is the main danger of constantly using an 'accommodating' (always giving in) style at work?

options.A: Building up personal resentment and professional burnout
options.C: Creating aggressive conflict with every team member

explanation: If you always say yes and push your own needs aside, you'll eventually burn out and feel quietly bitter. [learn more](GST321_U5_T4#GST321_U5_T4_h5)

question: Why might a nurse choose to use 'avoidance' during a heated ward argument?

options.A: To let intense emotions cool down before attempting discussion
options.B: To permanently ignore the underlying hospital policy
options.C: To prove that the other person was completely right
options.D: To win the argument without speaking a single word

explanation: Stepping away for a moment isn't always running away; sometimes it's the smartest way to let hot tempers cool off. [learn more](GST321_U5_T4#GST321_U5_T4_h6)

question: When does avoiding conflict turn into a real problem on a nursing unit?

options.A: When it is used during a fire drill or sudden cardiac arrest
options.B: When it is used for five minutes to let a colleague catch their breath
options.C: When it is used permanently to sweep serious problems under the rug
options.D: When it is applied to trivial, unimportant daily annoyances

explanation: Using avoidance as a permanent habit just hides serious issues until they blow up later. Problems need to be faced eventually! [learn more](GST321_U5_T4#GST321_U5_T4_h6)

question: In the DESC communication script, what does the letter 'D' stand for?
explanation: Always start by stating the facts of what you saw, without throwing blame or making personal attacks. [learn more](GST321_U5_T4#GST321_U5_T4_h7)

question: A nurse tells a colleague, 'I feel worried about patient safety when medications are left unlabeled.' What communication trick is being used here?

options.A: Avoiding the issue by changing the subject completely
options.B: Using an 'I' statement to express concern constructively
options.C: Accommodating the colleague's poor medication habits
options.D: Using a competing strategy to assert dominance

explanation: Starting with 'I feel' keeps the focus on your observations and patient safety instead of sounding like an attack on your coworker. [learn more](GST321_U5_T4#GST321_U5_T4_h7)

question: Why should you check back in after a conflict has supposedly been settled?

options.A: To punish anyone who failed to follow the new rules
options.B: To write a formal disciplinary report for the human resources file
options.C: To verify that the agreed solution is actually working in practice
options.D: To ensure the conflict is brought up again at the next meeting

explanation: Agreements look great on paper, but a quick follow-up ensures people are actually following through during busy shifts. [learn more](GST321_U5_T4#GST321_U5_T4_h8)

question: What does the term 'psychological safety' mean on a hospital ward?

options.A: A policy that prevents nurses from ever working night shifts
options.B: An environment where staff can speak up without fear of humiliation
options.C: A ward that has physical security guards stationed at every entrance
options.D: An agreement to never disagree with a physician's orders

explanation: Psychological safety means you can report mistakes, ask questions, and share concerns without worrying that someone will mock or punish you. [learn more](GST321_U5_T4#GST321_U5_T4_h8)
